p.src: Grandmother Jia returned from Lady Wang’s quarters and was naturally delighted to see Baoyu improving day by day. Fearing that Jia Zheng might summon him again, she had the head page among Jia Zheng’s personal attendants called in and instructed him: “If henceforth your master wishes to summon Baoyu for any occasion involving callers or guests, you need not come in to deliver the message. Tell him that I said this: first, the beating was severe, and the boy must spend several months recovering properly before he can walk about; second, the stars governing his fate are unfavorable, and after making offerings to them he must see no outsiders and may not pass beyond the inner gate until after the eighth month.” The head page received her orders and withdrew. Grandmother Jia then had Nanny Li, Xiren, and the others come and repeat this to Baoyu, so that he might set his mind at ease. Baoyu had always been reluctant to converse with scholars, officials, and other men, and especially detested ceremonial caps and robes and the formal exchange of congratulatory and condolence visits. Now that he had received this dispensation, he was more pleased than ever. Not only did he cut himself off entirely from relatives and friends, but even the customary morning and evening attendance upon his elders was left to his convenience. He spent each day roaming or lounging in the Garden, merely paying brief visits to Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang early every morning before returning. Yet he was always quite willing to perform errands for the maids and thus passed his days in perfect leisure. Whenever Baochai or one of the others tried tactfully to guide and admonish him, he would instead grow angry and declare, “What a fine, pure, spotless girl she was, yet she too has learned to fish for fame and angle for praise, joining the ranks of traitors to the realm and ghouls of official emolument! It all began when the men of old stirred up trouble for no reason, setting forth doctrines and coining phrases merely to lead astray the filthy, bearded creatures of later generations. Little did I imagine that I should be born so unfortunate as to see even the jeweled chambers and embroidered apartments tainted by this fashion. It truly betrays Heaven and Earth’s grace in gathering their finest essences to nurture such beauty!” Thus his wrath extended to the ancients, and apart from the Four Books, he actually burned all his other books. Seeing him behave so madly, no one spoke to him any longer about such serious matters. Only Lin Daiyu had never, from childhood onward, urged him to establish himself and win fame, and for this reason he held her in profound esteem.

p.src: But enough of this digression. We now return to Wang Xifeng. Since Jinchuan’s death, she had noticed that servants from several households often brought her gifts and came from time to time to pay their respects and flatter her. This aroused her suspicions, for she could not understand their purpose. That day someone brought her another gift. When no one else was present that evening, she smilingly asked Pinger, “Those families have little business with me. Why have they suddenly become so attentive?” Pinger gave a cold laugh. “Can’t you even think of that, ma’am? I expect their daughters are all maids in Her Ladyship’s apartments. At present Her Ladyship has four senior maids, each receiving an allowance of one tael a month, while all the rest receive only a few hundred cash. Now that Jinchuan is dead, they must be scheming to secure that profitable one-tael post.” Hearing this, Xifeng laughed. “Of course, of course! You have reminded me. These people are really far too greedy. They have made ample money, and no hard work falls upon them; it should be enough for them to put a daughter into service as their stand-in, yet they covet this as well. Never mind. Money from those families would not ordinarily find its way into my hands. Since they have brought this upon themselves, I shall accept whatever they send; in any case, I have a plan.” Having settled on this course, Xifeng deliberately kept postponing the matter. Only after those people had sent gifts to their hearts’ content did she find an opportunity to report it to Lady Wang.

p.src: At noon that day, Aunt Xue and her daughter, together with Lin Daiyu and the others, were eating in Lady Wang’s room. Seizing an opportunity, Xifeng said to Lady Wang, “Since Sister Jinchuan died, Your Ladyship has been one attendant short. If there is a maid whom Your Ladyship considers suitable, please give the order, so that her monthly allowance may be issued from next month.” Lady Wang considered this for a moment and replied, “In my view, what does precedent matter? There need not be exactly four or five. So long as there are enough to serve me, we might as well leave the vacancy unfilled.” Xifeng smiled. “In principle, Your Ladyship is quite right. Still, this is an old-established rule. Other apartments even have two such maids, while Your Ladyship alone would not observe the customary number. Besides, saving one tael of silver would make little difference.” Lady Wang thought again and said, “Very well. Continue drawing the allowance, but do not appoint another maid. Give the one tael of silver to Jinchuan’s younger sister Yuchuan instead. Her elder sister served me for a time but came to no good end. Since the younger sister remains in my service, it is not excessive for her to receive a double allowance.” Xifeng assented, then turned to find Yuchuan and said with a smile, “Wonderful news! Wonderful news!” Yuchuan came forward and kowtowed. Lady Wang asked, “There is something I have been meaning to ask you. How much do Concubine Zhao and Concubine Zhou receive each month now?” Xifeng replied, “The fixed allowance is two taels apiece. Concubine Zhao also receives two taels for young Master Huan, making four taels in all, plus four strings of cash.” Lady Wang asked, “Are they always paid the full amount?” Surprised by the question, Xifeng hastily replied, “Why would we not pay them the full amount?” Lady Wang said, “The other day I vaguely heard someone complaining that one string of cash was missing. What was the reason?” Xifeng quickly answered with a smile, “The maids serving the concubines were originally each allotted one string of cash a month. But last year the outside office decided that the allowance for each concubine’s maids should be halved to five hundred cash apiece. Since each concubine has two maids, that accounts for the missing string. They cannot blame me for that. I would gladly pay them myself, but the outside office withholds the money. Surely I cannot make up the difference out of my own pocket. I merely pass the money through my hands: I pay out whatever comes in and have no authority to decide the amount. Indeed, I spoke two or three times about restoring those two allowances to their former level. But they said the budget provided only that amount, so it was difficult for me to press the matter further. Now that the payments are in my hands, I do not even let them be a day late each month. When they used to collect it from the outside office, there was scarcely a month without some shortage or delay; they never once received it smoothly and without trouble.” Lady Wang let the matter rest when she heard this. After a while she asked again, “How many maids in the Old Lady’s apartments receive one tael?” “Eight,” replied Xifeng. “There are only seven there now; the eighth is Xiren.”

p.src: “That settles it,” said Lady Wang. “Your cousin Baoyu has no maid receiving an allowance of one tael either; Xiren is still counted as one of the Old Lady’s household.” “Xiren originally belonged to the Old Lady’s household,” Xifeng said with a smile. “She was merely assigned to serve Cousin Baoyu. Her one-tael allowance is still drawn from the allotment for the Old Lady’s maids. It would never do to cut that tael now on the grounds that Xiren belongs to Baoyu. If another maid is assigned to the Old Lady in her place, then her allowance may be cut. But if it is not cut, another maid must be added to Cousin Huan’s rooms as well, for only then would matters be fair and even. Even the seven senior maids, including Qingwen and Sheyue, each receive one string of cash a month, while the eight junior maids, including Jiahui, each receive five hundred cash a month—all by the Old Lady’s own order. What right has anyone else to be angry or resentful?” Aunt Xue laughed. “Just listen to that tongue of Feng’s! It rattles on like a cartload of walnuts overturning, yet her accounts are perfectly clear and her reasoning perfectly fair.” “Auntie, surely I haven’t said anything wrong?” Xifeng asked with a smile. “Nothing you said was wrong,” Aunt Xue replied, laughing. “But wouldn’t you spare yourself some effort if you spoke a little more slowly?” Xifeng was about to laugh, but hurriedly restrained herself and waited for Lady Wang’s instructions. Lady Wang pondered for a long while before saying to Xifeng, “Tomorrow, choose a good maid and send her to serve the Old Lady in Xiren’s place, then remove Xiren’s present allotment. From my own monthly allowance of twenty taels, set aside two taels and one string of cash for Xiren. Henceforth, whatever is provided for Concubine Zhao and Concubine Zhou is to be provided for Xiren too; only Xiren’s share must all come out of my own allowance, without drawing upon the household funds.” Xifeng assented to each instruction, then playfully nudged Aunt Xue and said, “You heard that, Auntie. What have I always told you? Today my words have come true exactly.” “It should have been done long ago,” said Aunt Xue. Her looks naturally go without saying, but what is truly rare is her generous way of conducting herself and the blend of warmth, firmness, and strength of character with which she speaks to everyone.” With tears in her eyes, Lady Wang said, “How could any of you know all the good qualities of that child Xiren? She is ten times better than my Baoyu! If Baoyu is truly blessed enough to have her serve him faithfully for the rest of his life, I shall ask for nothing more.” “If that is how you feel,” said Xifeng, “why not have her face threaded and openly install her in his rooms as his concubine?”

p.src: After the conversation had ended and some time had passed in silence, Xifeng saw that there was nothing more to discuss and turned to leave. She had only just reached the veranda when she saw several stewards’ wives waiting to report household matters to her. When she emerged, they all smiled and asked, “What business have you been reporting today, madam, to keep you in there so long? You must have been overcome by the heat.” Xifeng rolled her sleeves up several turns, stepped onto the threshold of the side gate, and said with a smile, “The through-breeze here is pleasantly cool. I shall stand in it awhile before going on.” Then she told them, “You wonder why I spent so long reporting. Her Ladyship recalled matters from two hundred years ago and questioned me about every one of them. How could I refuse to answer?” She gave a cold laugh. “From now on, I really shall do a few cruel things. Let them complain of me to Her Ladyship—I am not afraid. You muddle-headed, rotten-tongued, lowborn wretches who deserve a miserable death—stop dreaming your damned sweet dreams! There will be plenty of days ahead when everything is docked from you at once. Now that the maids’ allowances have been cut, they blame us for it. They never stop to consider what sort of slaves they are, or whether they deserve to have two or three maids of their own!” Still cursing as she went, she finally departed to choose a maid and report back to Grandmother Jia; of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Meanwhile, after Lady Wang and the others had finished their watermelon and chatted idly for a while, they finally went their separate ways. Baochai, Daiyu, and the others returned to the Garden. Baochai invited Daiyu to join her at Lotus Fragrance Pavilion, but Daiyu said she was about to bathe, so they parted company. Baochai walked on alone and, since it lay along her way, entered Happy Red Court, intending to seek out Baoyu for some conversation to dispel her afternoon drowsiness. To her surprise, the moment she entered the courtyard she found it utterly silent; even the two cranes were asleep beneath the banana plants. Baochai followed the covered walk into the house and saw the maids sprawled every which way, asleep on the beds in the outer room. Passing around the many-paneled partition, she entered Baoyu's room. Baoyu lay asleep on the bed. Xiren sat beside him sewing, with a white rhinoceros-hair fly whisk lying nearby. Baochai came closer and said with a quiet laugh, “You are really far too careful. There are no flies or mosquitoes in this room, so what are you chasing with that fly whisk?” Caught unawares, Xiren looked up with a start and saw Baochai. She hurriedly put down her sewing, rose, and whispered with a smile, “You have come, miss! I wasn't expecting you and you gave me such a fright. You don't know, miss: though there are no flies or mosquitoes, some tiny insect or other slips in through the holes in the gauze. You cannot even see it, but once you fall asleep it bites you, and it pinches like an ant.” “No wonder,” said Baochai. “Behind this house you are close to the water and surrounded by fragrant flowers, while the room itself is sweet-scented too. Those insects breed in the hearts of flowers and are drawn wherever they smell fragrance.” As she spoke, she examined Xiren's needlework. It was a white satin bellyband lined in red, embroidered with mandarin ducks sporting among lotuses: red blossoms, green leaves, and brilliantly colored birds. “Oh, what bright and beautiful work!” exclaimed Baochai. “Who is it for, that it merits so much labor?” Xiren pursed her lips toward the bed. Baochai laughed. “At his age, does he still wear one of these?” Xiren laughed. “He normally refuses to wear one. That is why I am making this one especially fine: once he sees it, he will not be able to resist wearing it. The weather is hot now, and he is so careless when he sleeps. If I coax him into putting it on, there will be no cause for concern even if his covers slip off at night. You think this one took a great deal of work, but you have not yet seen the one he is wearing now.” Baochai laughed. “You really are wonderfully patient.” “I have worked so much on it today,” said Xiren, “that my neck is terribly sore from bending over.” Then she added with a smile, “Dear miss, please sit here for a little while. I will go out for a walk and be back presently.” With that, she left.

p.src: Now Daiyu had happened to meet Xiangyun, who invited her to come and congratulate Xiren. When the two reached the courtyard and found it utterly quiet, Xiangyun turned aside and went first to look for Xiren in the side room. Daiyu went to the window and peered through its gauze. She saw Baoyu, dressed in a silvery-red gauze jacket, lying at ease asleep on the bed, while Baochai sat beside him sewing, with the fly whisk lying nearby. At this sight Daiyu quickly drew back, covered her mouth to stifle her laughter, and beckoned to Xiangyun. Seeing Daiyu behave so mysteriously, Xiangyun assumed there must be some amusing novelty and hurried over to look. She too was about to laugh when she suddenly remembered how kindly Baochai had always treated her, and hastily covered her mouth. Knowing that Daiyu never spared anyone and fearing she would make some cutting jest, Xiangyun quickly pulled her away, saying, “Let us go. I remember Xiren said she meant to wash clothes at the pond this afternoon. She must have gone there, so let us look for her there.” Daiyu understood perfectly. She gave two cold laughs but had no choice except to follow her away.

Seeing Daiyu behave so mysteriously, Xiangyun assumed there must be some amusing novelty and hurried over to look. She too was about to laugh when she suddenly remembered how kindly Baochai had always treated her, and hastily covered her mouth.
Knowing that Daiyu never spared anyone and fearing she would make some cutting jest, Xiangyun quickly pulled her away, saying, “Let us go.
I remember Xiren said she meant to wash clothes at the pond this afternoon. She must have gone there, so let us look for her there.”
Daiyu understood perfectly. She gave two cold laughs but had no choice except to follow her away.

p.src: Baochai had embroidered only two or three petals when Baoyu suddenly cried out angrily in his sleep, “How can anyone believe what monks and Taoist priests say? What ‘marriage of gold and jade’? I say it is the marriage of wood and stone!” Hearing these words, Xue Baochai was involuntarily stunned. Just then Xiren came over and said with a smile, “He still has not woken?” Baochai shook her head. Xiren smiled again. “I just ran into Miss Lin and Miss Shi. Did they come in here?” “I did not see them come in,” replied Baochai. Then she asked Xiren with a smile, “Did they not tell you something?” Xiren laughed. “It could only have been their usual joking. What serious business could they have to discuss?” Baochai laughed. “What they said was no joke. I was just about to tell you when you hurried out.”

p.src: Before she had finished speaking, a maid sent by Xifeng arrived to summon Xiren. Baochai smiled. “It must be about that very matter.” Xiren had no choice but to wake two maids and, leaving Happy Red Court together with Baochai, make her way to Xifeng’s quarters. Sure enough, Xifeng told her the news, then instructed her to kowtow to Lady Wang, saying that she need not yet go to see Grandmother Jia; all this left Xiren feeling rather embarrassed. After paying her respects to Lady Wang, she hurried back. Baoyu was already awake and asked what had happened. Xiren answered evasively for the moment and did not tell him until night had fallen and all was quiet. Baoyu was beside himself with delight and said to her with a smile, “Now let me see whether you’ll go home again! The last time you went home, you came back saying your brother meant to redeem you, that you had no secure future here, and what would become of you in the end—frightening me with all those heartless, distant words. From now on, I should like to see who dares tell you to leave.” Xiren gave a cold laugh. “You had better not speak so soon. From now on I belong to Her Ladyship. If I wish to leave, I need not even tell you; I have only to inform Her Ladyship, and off I go.” Baoyu smiled. “Even supposing I behaved badly and you reported it to Her Ladyship and simply left, once others heard you had gone because I treated you badly, you would hardly feel easy about it either.” Xiren laughed. “Why should I feel uneasy? If you turned bandit or thief, would I have to follow you even then? Besides, there is always death. Even if one lives to a hundred, death must come in the end. Once this breath is gone, I shall neither hear nor see, and that will be the end of it.” At these words Baoyu hastily covered her mouth with his hand. “Enough, enough, enough! Say no more of that.” Xiren knew well how peculiar Baoyu’s temperament was: flattering, auspicious words disgusted him as hollow and unreal, yet unreserved truths like these made him melancholy. Regretting that she had spoken too bluntly, she quickly smiled and changed the subject, choosing only matters Baoyu had always enjoyed discussing. First she asked him about spring breezes and autumn moons, then they spoke of pale powder and gleaming rouge; next they discussed the goodness of girls, until the talk turned to girls dying, whereupon Xiren hurriedly covered her mouth. Baoyu was speaking with mounting animation when he saw that she had fallen silent. He smiled and said, “Who does not die? What matters is to die well. Those foul creatures with whiskers know only that civil officials should die remonstrating and military officers should die in battle, regarding these two deaths as worthy of great men who die for fame and honor. Yet how could that be better than not dying at all! Only when there is a benighted ruler does a minister have cause to remonstrate; yet intent solely upon winning fame, he recklessly throws away his life—and in what position does that leave his sovereign? Only when war breaks out does a soldier have cause to fight; yet recklessly throwing away his life, intent solely upon earning glory on the battlefield, in what position does that leave his country? Therefore none of these is a proper death.” Xiren said, “Loyal ministers and able generals die only when they have no other choice.”

p.src: Baoyu replied, “Those military officers merely rely on hot-blooded courage. Poor in planning and wanting in strategy, they lose their lives through their own incompetence. Can that really be called unavoidable? Civil officials are even worse than military men. They learn a few lines from books and lodge them in their minds; then, if the court shows the slightest flaw, they spout nonsense and offer reckless remonstrance, caring only to win a reputation for loyalty and martyrdom. When their turbid passions surge, they throw away their lives on the spot. Can that really be called unavoidable? Besides, you must remember that the court rules by the Mandate of Heaven. If the sovereign were neither sagacious nor benevolent, Heaven and Earth would never have entrusted him with the myriad weighty affairs of state. Thus it is clear that all those who died were merely seeking fame and understood nothing of true righteousness. Suppose that fortune truly favored me, and that this were the appointed time for me to die. If I died now while all of you were here, and if the tears you wept for me could swell into a great river, lift up my corpse, and carry it to some secluded place beyond the reach of crow or sparrow, where it might dissolve upon the wind, and if thereafter I never had to be reborn as a human being—then I should have died at the right time.” When Xiren suddenly heard him uttering such wild nonsense, she hastily said that she was sleepy and ignored him. Only then did Baoyu close his eyes and fall asleep; by the next day he too had put the matter from his mind.

p.src: One day, having grown weary of roaming from place to place, Baoyu thought of the songs from The Peony Pavilion. He read them through twice by himself, but still felt unsatisfied. He had heard that among the twelve girls of Pear-Blossom Court, Lingguan, who played young female roles, sang best of all. He therefore went deliberately out through the side gate in search of her and found Baoguan and Yuguan in the courtyard. When they saw him, they smilingly invited him to sit down. Baoyu asked, “Where is Lingguan by herself?” They all told him, “She is in her room.” Baoyu hurried to her room and found Lingguan lying alone with her head on the pillow. When he entered, she did not stir in the least. Baoyu was accustomed to frolicking freely with the other girls and assumed that Lingguan was no different. He went forward and sat beside her, then coaxed her with an ingratiating smile to get up and sing the entire “Wavering Silken Threads in the Clear Air” sequence. But as soon as Lingguan saw him sit down, she hastily raised herself and drew away. With a grave expression she said, “My voice is hoarse. The other day, when Her Highness summoned us to the palace, even then I did not sing.” When Baoyu saw her sitting upright and looked at her more closely, he realized that she was the very girl who had traced the character “Qiang” beneath the rose trellis that day. Confronted with such treatment, he felt for the first time in his life what it was to be rejected and disliked. His face reddened awkwardly, and he had no choice but to leave. Baoguan and the others could not understand what had happened and asked him the reason. Baoyu told them what had occurred and then went out. Baoguan said, “Just wait a little while. When Second Master Qiang comes and asks her to sing, she will certainly do it.” This puzzled Baoyu. “Where has Brother Qiang gone?” he asked. Baoguan replied, “He only just went out. Lingguan must have wanted something again, and he has gone to find it for her.”

p.src: Baoyu found this curious. After waiting a little while, he did indeed see Jia Qiang coming in from outside, cheerfully carrying a birdcage fitted with a tiny stage and containing a bird, as he went inside looking for Lingguan. Seeing Baoyu, he had no choice but to stop. Baoyu asked him, “What kind of bird is it? Can it carry flags and perform on the stage?” Jia Qiang replied with a smile, “It is a jade-crested golden bean.” “How much did it cost?” Baoyu asked. “One tael and eight mace of silver,” said Jia Qiang. As he spoke, he invited Baoyu to sit down and went into Lingguan’s room himself. By now Baoyu had lost all desire to hear her sing; he wanted instead to see how Jia Qiang and Lingguan behaved together. He saw Jia Qiang go in and say with a smile, “Get up and look at this plaything.” Lingguan sat up and asked what it was. Jia Qiang said, “I bought you a bird to play with, so you need not be gloomy every day with nothing to cheer you. Let me make it perform for you first.” With that, he used some millet to coax the bird into darting about the stage and carrying little flags painted with demon faces. All the girls laughed and called it amusing, but Lingguan alone gave two cold laughs and lay down again in a huff. Jia Qiang continued smiling ingratiatingly and asked whether she liked it. Lingguan said, “It was not enough for your family to bring decent human beings here and shut us in this prison to learn this wretched trade; now you have brought a bird here and made it do precisely the same thing. You plainly brought it to mock us by showing us our own likeness, yet you still ask whether I like it.” Hearing this, Jia Qiang grew alarmed and hurriedly swore solemn oaths of his innocence. Then he said, “What possessed my addled head today! I spent a tael or two buying it only to relieve your boredom; the thought never crossed my mind. Enough, enough—I shall set it free, and may that help ward off your illness and misfortune.” With that, he truly released the bird and smashed the cage to pieces. Lingguan went on, “Though that bird is not human, it too has an old mother bird waiting in the nest. How could you bear to capture it and make it perform this wretched trick! Today I coughed up two mouthfuls of blood, and Madam sent for a doctor to examine me. Instead of asking carefully about my condition, you brought this thing to amuse yourself at my expense. Of course, no one cares for me or looks after me—and on top of that I have to fall ill.” As she spoke, she began to cry again. Jia Qiang hastily said, “I asked the doctor last night, and he said it was nothing serious. He said you should take two doses of medicine, and he would examine you again the day after tomorrow. Who could have known you would cough up blood again today? I shall fetch him now.” With that, he made ready to go for the doctor. “Stop!” Lingguan called again. “If you rush out in a temper under this scorching sun to fetch him now, I will refuse to see him when he comes.” Hearing her say this, Jia Qiang had no choice but to stop again.

p.src: Baoyu pondered and deliberated all the way back, returning dazedly to Happy Red Court, where Lin Daiyu and Xiren happened to be sitting together in conversation. As soon as he entered, Baoyu heaved a long sigh before Xiren and said, “What I said last night was utterly wrong. No wonder Father called me a frog peering at the sky from the bottom of a well and measuring the sea with a shell. Last night I said that all your tears would be shed to mourn me, but that was wrong. I cannot possibly have them all. From now on, each person shall receive only the tears destined for him.” Xiren’s words the night before had been no more than playful banter, and she had already forgotten them. Surprised that Baoyu should bring them up again today, she laughed and said, “You truly are a little mad.” Baoyu made no reply. From that time on, he understood deeply that every bond of affection in human life has its allotted destiny, though he often grieved in secret: “Who, in years to come, will shed tears over my grave?” These were all thoughts harbored in Baoyu’s heart, and we should not speculate too freely about them.

p.src: Now Lin Daiyu, seeing Baoyu in this state, knew that something elsewhere had bewitched him again. Since it was not convenient to question him further, she said, “I just heard while I was with Aunt that tomorrow is Aunt Xue’s birthday. She asked me to stop by and ask whether you mean to go. Send someone ahead to give them word.” Baoyu said, “Last time I did not even attend Elder Master’s birthday. If I go now, what if I run into people there? I am not going anywhere at all. In such dreadful heat I would have to dress formally too. Aunt surely would not be angry if I stayed away.” Xiren hastened to say, “What sort of talk is that? She is not to be compared with Elder Master. She lives nearby and is a relative besides. If you do not go, will she not wonder why? If you fear the heat, just go there early in the morning, make your birthday obeisance, drink a cup of tea, and return. Would that not look proper?” Before Baoyu could answer, Daiyu laughed and said, “Considering that she drove the mosquitoes away for you, you ought at least to pay them a visit.” Puzzled, Baoyu quickly asked, “What do you mean, drove the mosquitoes away?” Xiren then told him how, while he slept yesterday with no one to keep him company, Miss Bao had sat with him for a while. Hearing this, Baoyu hurriedly said, “That was wrong of me. How could I have fallen asleep and shown her such disrespect?” At the same time, he added, “I shall certainly go tomorrow.” While they were speaking, Shi Xiangyun suddenly appeared, neatly and fully dressed, to take her leave, saying that her family had sent someone to fetch her. Hearing this, Baoyu and Lin Daiyu quickly rose and invited her to sit down. Shi Xiangyun would not sit, so Baoyu and Daiyu had no choice but to escort her toward the front. Shi Xiangyun’s eyes brimmed with tears, but with members of her household present, she dared not show the full depth of her distress. Presently Xue Baochai hurried over, making their affectionate reluctance to part even harder to bear. Baochai alone understood the situation clearly: if Xiangyun’s attendants returned and reported matters to her aunt, Xiangyun might be ill-treated when she got home. Baochai therefore urged her to leave. Everyone escorted her as far as the inner gate. Baoyu wanted to accompany her farther, but Xiangyun stopped him. A moment later she turned, called Baoyu to her side, and whispered, “Even if Grandmother does not remember me, you must mention me often and have someone sent to fetch me here.” Baoyu promised her again and again that he would. Only after watching her climb into the carriage and depart did everyone go back inside. To learn what happened next, listen to the explanation in the following chapter.
